chunks.breadcrumb_text: [WHO 2024 Guideline | Glossary of terms | Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) | Page vii-ix]

Term: Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT)
Definition: A medical product that supplies a controlled amount of nicotine to the body for a limited period, to help quit tobacco use completely. NRT is used to replace the nicotine the body receives through smoking cigarettes or using other tobacco products, and they deliver nicotine without the harmful chemicals present in tobacco smoke or smokeless tobacco. NRT helps to reduce the craving for tobacco and lessens the severity of nicotine withdrawals, thus making it easier for users to quit tobacco use. NRT products include nicotine gum, patches, lozenges, inhalers, and nasal or mouth sprays.

chunks.heading_path: Front Matter > Glossary of terms > Tobacco cessation
chunks.breadcrumb_text: [WHO 2024 Guideline | Glossary of terms | Tobacco cessation | Page vii-ix]
chunks.content:
Term: Tobacco cessation
Definition: The process of stopping the use of any tobacco product, with or without assistance. May also be referred to as abstinence or quitting. There are multiple technical definitions that vary from study to study. The strictest definition is “no use of combustible or smokeless tobacco products or any other nicotine and tobacco products for at least 6 months”. Abstinence/quitting can be measured by “point prevalence abstinence” meaning the person has complete abstinence during a designated time period (for example, 7 or 30 days) prior to assessment, or prolonged abstinence (complete abstinence after an initial grace period), or continuous abstinence (complete abstinence beginning on the target quit day and lasting until the assessment).

chunks.heading_path: Front Matter > Executive summary > Background & Objectives
chunks.breadcrumb_text: [WHO 2024 Guideline | Executive summary | Pages xi-xii]
chunks.content:
Background
Tobacco kills more than 8 million people per year and imposes a significant economic burden throughout the world. Globally, there are still 1.25 billion people who use tobacco. Intensive and sustained efforts are needed to end this global epidemic. As tobacco control policy efforts increase, the scaling up of comprehensive tobacco cessation services to support current tobacco users to quit is imperative.

Rationale and objectives
The need to help tobacco users quit as a key component of a comprehensive tobacco control approach has been recognized by the WHO FCTC. Evidence to inform the guideline recommendations was derived from 20 existing or newly commissioned systematic reviews. The GDG reviewed the evidence and made recommendations using the GRADE approach.

chunks.heading_path: Front Matter > Executive summary > Summary of recommendations
chunks.breadcrumb_text: [WHO 2024 Guideline | Executive summary | Summary of Recommendations List | Pages xii-xiv]
chunks.content:
Summary of recommendations (Executive Summary List):
1. WHO recommends brief advice (between 30 seconds and 3 minutes per encounter) be delivered routinely for all tobacco users in health-care settings by health-care providers. (Strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence)
2. WHO recommends more-intensive behavioural support be offered to all tobacco users interested in quitting, including individual, group or telephone counselling. (Strong recommendation; moderate-certainty evidence)
3. WHO suggests digital tobacco cessation interventions, such as text messaging, smartphone apps and AI-based software, may be offered. (Conditional recommendation; low to very low-certainty evidence)
4. WHO recommends varenicline, NRT, bupropion and cytisine as pharmacological treatments for tobacco cessation. (Strong recommendation; high to moderate-certainty evidence)
5. WHO recommends combination NRT (e.g. patch plus fast-acting form) as first-line treatment. (Strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence)
6. WHO recommends providing intensive behavioural support interventions for smokeless tobacco use cessation. (Strong recommendation; low-certainty evidence)
7. WHO recommends varenicline or NRT as pharmacological options for smokeless tobacco use cessation. (Strong recommendation for varenicline, conditional for NRT)
8. WHO recommends combining pharmacotherapy and behavioural interventions for tobacco cessation. (Strong recommendation; moderate-certainty evidence)
9. Evidence is insufficient to make a recommendation for or against traditional, complementary and alternative therapies. (Statement; very low-certainty evidence)
10. WHO recommends that all health-care facilities include tobacco use status in medical records (including EHRs). (Strong recommendation; low-certainty evidence)
11. WHO recommends training of all health-care providers on delivery of evidence-based tobacco cessation interventions. (Strong recommendation; low-certainty evidence)
12. WHO recommends that evidence-based tobacco cessation interventions be provided at no cost or reduced cost to tobacco users. (Strong recommendation; low-certainty evidence)

chunks.content:
3.1.3. Justification and evidence:
Evidence from Cochrane systematic reviews demonstrates that brief advice significantly increases quit rates compared with no advice (RR: 1.25; 95% CI: 1.14–1.36; 44 trials; 28 439 participants). For intensive individual counselling, evidence shows increased quitting compared with minimal support (RR: 1.57; 95% CI: 1.40–1.77; 33 trials; 13 762 participants). For group counselling, long-term quitting increased (RR: 1.88; 95% CI: 1.52–2.33; 66 RCTs; 4395 participants). For proactive telephone counselling, quit rates significantly increased compared with self-help or standard care (RR: 1.25; 95% CI: 1.15–1.35; 104 studies; 111 653 participants).

• National strategic plans for tobacco control must integrate clinical cessation into broader WHO FCTC MPOWER policies (tobacco taxation, smoke-free public spaces, graphic health warnings, advertising bans).

• Safeguard all tobacco cessation policies and services from tobacco industry interference in accordance with WHO FCTC Article 5.3.

chunks.breadcrumb_text: [WHO 2024 Guideline | Annexes > Annex 2: Additional information for implementing the recommendations > Annex 2 > Pharmacological interventions | Pages 49-51]
chunks.content:
Annex 2: Additional information for implementing Pharmacological interventions:
• Minimal medication availability in all countries: at least one long-acting NRT, one short-acting NRT, and one α4β2 agonist (varenicline or cytisine).
• Special clinical populations: Adults with psychiatric conditions are at higher risk of relapse and benefit from longer, combined treatments with symptom monitoring. For adolescents, evidence is insufficient for routine pharmacotherapy prescribing.
• Varenicline and Cytisine details: Varenicline is titrated up prior to quit date to minimize nausea. Cytisine offers a cost-effective plant-based alternative with similar receptor binding affinity.
